stages.name: Government intervention: taxes
stages.title: Government intervention: taxes
stages.sub: After this the student can explain why governments tax negative externalities and what benefits this brings.

steps.q: A government puts a £2 per litre tax on petrol. Petrol firms now hand over £2 for every litre they sell. Who ends up collecting money from this?
steps.hint: Think about who the tax is paid to, not who charges the price at the pump.
steps.pre: So a tax paid to the government on every unit sold generates

steps.q: Burning petrol pollutes the air, harming people who never bought any petrol. If the government taxes petrol so its price rises closer to the true harm it causes, what happens to the gap between the price drivers pay and the cost to society?
steps.right: It shrinks, price moves closer to the true cost
steps.wrong: It stays the same, only revenue changes
steps.hint: The externality was that price ignored harm to others. Does taxing it force that harm into the price?
steps.pre: Making buyers face the full social cost like this is called

steps.q: If a tax pushes the market price up towards the true cost to society, does the third-party harm from overconsumption get smaller?
steps.right: Yes, it reduces the market failure
steps.wrong: No, the harm is unrelated to price
steps.hint: You already saw the tax closes the gap between private price and social cost. What does that do to the harm caused by overconsumption?

steps.q: Petrol is now taxed and more expensive, but electric cars are not taxed at all. Do firms and drivers gain a reason to shift towards electric cars and cleaner engines?
steps.right: Yes, the untaxed alternative becomes relatively more attractive
steps.wrong: No, the tax has no effect on which technology people choose
